title: Kinetic Energy in Classical Mechanics
short_intro: Kinetic energy is the scalar energy possessed by a body due to its translational or rotational motion. It represents the total work required to accelerate a body from rest to its current velocity.

exam_scope.tgt_core: Definition, units, dimensional formula, work-energy theorem for rectilinear motion, simple numericals involving mass and velocity, and relation between linear momentum and kinetic energy.
exam_scope.pgt_extension: Relativistic kinetic energy, rotational kinetic energy, rolling motion combining translation and rotation, work-energy theorem in non-inertial frames, and kinetic energy expressed in generalized coordinates.

prerequisites: Work and scalar product of vectors

concept_notes.heading: Definition and Physical Nature
bullets: Kinetic energy (KE) is a scalar quantity dependent on the reference frame.
Its dimensional formula is [M L<sup>2</sup> T<sup>-2</sup>] and the SI unit is the Joule (J).
It is always non-negative for a real particle in classical mechanics.

concept_notes.heading: Work-Energy Theorem
bullets: The net work done by all forces acting on a particle equals the change in its kinetic energy.
Expressed mathematically as W<sub>net</sub> = ΔKE = KE<sub>final</sub> - KE<sub>initial</sub>.
Holds true for both constant and variable forces in inertial reference frames.

concept_notes.heading: Relation with Linear Momentum
bullets: For a particle of mass m moving with linear momentum p, KE = p<sup>2</sup> / (2m).
If momentum is doubled at constant mass, kinetic energy increases by a factor of four.
For a system of particles, total kinetic energy is the sum of translational KE of the centre of mass and internal KE relative to the centre of mass.

concept_notes.heading: Rotational and Combined Kinetic Energy
bullets: A rigid body rotating about a fixed axis possesses rotational kinetic energy equal to (1/2)Iω<sup>2</sup>.
A body undergoing simultaneous translation and rotation has total kinetic energy KE = (1/2)Mv<sub>cm</sub><sup>2</sup> + (1/2)I<sub>cm</sub>ω<sup>2</sup>.
In relativistic mechanics, kinetic energy is given by KE = (γ - 1)mc<sup>2</sup>.

derivations.title: Work-Energy Relation for Rectilinear Motion
derivations.conditions: Particle of mass m moving along a straight line under a net force F
steps: Start with Newton's second law: F = m(dv/dt) = m(dv/dx)(dx/dt) = mv(dv/dx).
Integrate force with respect displacement x from initial position x<sub>1</sub> to final position x<sub>2</sub>: W = ∫ F dx = ∫ mv (dv/dx) dx.
Change the integration variable from displacement to velocity: W = ∫<sub>v<sub>1</sub></sub><sup>v<sub>2</sub></sup> mv dv.

derivations.title: Rotational Kinetic Energy of a Rigid Body
derivations.conditions: Rigid body rotating about a fixed axis with angular velocity ω
steps: Consider the rigid body as a collection of point masses m<sub>i</sub> at perpendicular distances r<sub>i</sub> from the axis of rotation.
The linear speed of the i-th particle is v<sub>i</sub> = r<sub>i</sub>ω.
The total kinetic energy is the scalar sum of the kinetic energies of all individual particles: KE = ∑ (1/2) m<sub>i</sub> v<sub>i</sub><sup>2</sup>.
Substitute v<sub>i</sub>: KE = ∑ (1/2) m<sub>i</sub> (r<sub>i</sub>ω)<sup>2</sup> = (1/2) (∑ m<sub>i</sub> r<sub>i</sub><sup>2</sup>) ω<sup>2</sup>.
Identify the term in parentheses as the moment of inertia I = ∑ m<sub>i</sub> r<sub>i</sub><sup>2</sup>.

formula_sheet.name: Rotational Kinetic Energy
formula_sheet.variables: I = moment of inertia, \omega = angular velocity

formula_sheet.name: Total Kinetic Energy of Rolling Motion
formula_sheet.variables: M = total mass, v_{cm} = velocity of centre of mass, I_{cm} = moment of inertia about centre of mass, \omega = angular velocity

formula_sheet.name: Work-Energy Theorem
formula_sheet.variables: W_{net} = net work done, \Delta KE = change in kinetic energy

formula_sheet.name: Relativistic Kinetic Energy
formula_sheet.variables: \gamma = Lorentz factor (1 / \sqrt{1 - v^2/c^2}), m = rest mass, c = speed of light
formula_sheet.conditions: High velocities approaching speed of light

formula_sheet.name: Kinetic Energy of System of Particles
formula_sheet.variables: M = total mass, v_{cm} = velocity of centre of mass, v_i' = velocity relative to centre of mass

graphs_and_experiments.title: Kinetic Energy versus Velocity (Classical vs Relativistic)
graphs_and_experiments.what_to_draw: A 2D plot with velocity v on the horizontal axis and kinetic energy on the vertical axis. Draw a parabolic curve for classical KE = (1/2)mv^2 and an asymptotically rising curve for relativistic KE.
graphs_and_experiments.interpretation: Classical KE grows quadratically with velocity and is valid for v << c. Relativistic KE approaches infinity as v approaches c.
graphs_and_experiments.exam_use: Tested in conceptual multiple-choice questions regarding validity limits of classical mechanics.

graphs_and_experiments.title: Kinetic Energy versus Momentum
graphs_and_experiments.what_to_draw: A parabolic curve plotting KE on the vertical axis against momentum p on the horizontal axis for a constant mass.
graphs_and_experiments.interpretation: Since KE = p^2 / (2m), the curve is a parabola opening upwards with slope dependent on 1/(2m).
graphs_and_experiments.exam_use: Frequently used in numerical problems evaluating percentage change in kinetic energy when momentum is altered.

graphs_and_experiments.title: Work-Energy Verification Experiment (Inclined Plane)
graphs_and_experiments.what_to_draw: Schematic diagram of a trolley rolling down an inclined track with photogates measuring velocity at two points.
graphs_and_experiments.interpretation: Verifies that the work done by the component of gravitational force along the incline equals the experimentally measured gain in translational kinetic energy.
graphs_and_experiments.exam_use: Core practical physics concept underpinning experimental mechanics questions.

solved_numericals.question: A body of mass 2 kg has a linear momentum of 10 kg m/s. Calculate its kinetic energy.
solution_steps: Identify given values: mass m = 2 kg, momentum p = 10 kg m/s.
Use the formula relating kinetic energy and momentum: KE = p^2 / (2m).

solved_numericals.question: If the linear momentum of a body is increased by 50%, find the percentage increase in its kinetic energy.
solution_steps: Let initial momentum be p_1 = p and initial kinetic energy be KE_1 = p^2 / (2m).
Percentage increase = [(KE_2 - KE_1) / KE_1] * 100 = [(2.25 KE_1 - KE_1) / KE_1] * 100 = 125%.

solved_numericals.question: A solid cylinder of mass 4 kg and radius 0.1 m rolls without slipping on a horizontal surface with a translational velocity of 2 m/s. Calculate its total kinetic energy.
solution_steps: Identify given parameters: M = 4 kg, R = 0.1 m, v = 2 m/s.
For a solid cylinder, the moment of inertia about its central axis is I = (1/2) M R^2.
For rolling without slipping, angular velocity ω = v / R.

assumptions_and_limitations: Classical kinetic energy formula ((1/2)mv^2) assumes speeds are significantly smaller than the speed of light in vacuum (v << c).
Assumes the observer is in an inertial frame of reference; in non-inertial frames, pseudo forces must be accounted for in the work-energy theorem.

common_misconceptions.wrong: Kinetic energy is an absolute property of a body regardless of the observer.
common_misconceptions.correct: Kinetic energy is frame-dependent and varies depending on the velocity of the observer's reference frame.
common_misconceptions.why: Velocity depends on the chosen frame of reference, hence KE = (1/2)mv^2 yields different values for different observers.

common_misconceptions.wrong: If the net work done on a body is zero, its velocity must be zero.
common_misconceptions.correct: If net work is zero, the change in kinetic energy is zero, meaning speed remains constant, but velocity vector may change direction (as in uniform circular motion).
common_misconceptions.why: Work depends on displacement and force along the displacement, whereas speed can remain constant while direction changes.

quick_revision: Kinetic energy is a scalar quantity given by KE = (1/2)mv^2 = p^2/(2m) in classical mechanics.
Translational Kinetic Energy: KE = \frac{1}{2} m v^2
